meta.claim: defendant A (claim): the stream state graph is endpoint-role symmetric -- swapping the two endpoint roles (local <-> remote) maps every arrow to an arrow: reserved (local) <-> reserved (remote) (server-push reservation twins), half-closed (local) <-> half-closed (remote), with idle, open and closed fixed. The RFC writes the two reserved states and the two half-closed states as mirror bullet lists, and the RST escape says verbatim 'Either endpoint can send a RST_STREAM frame' in both reserved states.
meta.construction: order-2 group: swap reserved (local) <-> reserved (remote) (states 1 <-> 2) AND half-closed (local) <-> half-closed (remote) (states 4 <-> 5)
meta.why_it_looks_legal: on the unlabeled graph every edge maps to an edge: idle->res(l)/res(r) are twins, res(l)->hc(r) mirrors res(r)->hc(l), open->hc(l)/hc(r) are twins, and every ->closed edge has its twin
meta.why_it_is_not_a_symmetry: the labels move with the roles: 'send PP' on idle->reserved (local) becomes 'recv PP' on idle->reserved (remote); likewise send H/recv H, send ES/recv ES and send R/recv R differ on most edges, so with event names pinned the swap fails -- the two roles are complementary, not identical
meta.engineering_anchor: the RFC defines the state machine once and lets both endpoints use it subjectively: 'Both endpoints have a subjective view of the state of a stream' (sec.5.1); the mirror reading is exactly how one shared diagram serves both sides
meta.semantics_note: event-class model: semantics declared "fixed" (protocol-true reading); the relabel row is the diagnostic contrast reading
